new_statements.translation: Yaouré has four basic distinctive level tones: high, mid-high, mid-low, low. [...] The tone schemes of lexical bases are built from these level tones. — One observes that Yaouré has four distinctive pitch levels, i.e. four level tonemes: high (H), mid-high (MH), mid-low (MB), and low (B) [...]. The tonemes just identified are level tonemes, in the sense that only constant relative pitch carries the distinctive function.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Yaouré is a four-level-tone language (H, MH, MB, B, with tone schemes per syllable type and rules of tone spreading, raising, lowering, dissimilation and copying). The source says nothing at all about word stress, accent or prominence; no stress rule can be extracted.
new_statements.exceptions: None relevant; the thesis discusses tone-scheme changes in inflection and compounding, not stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Lexical bases (CV, CVV, CVLV, CVCV) in citation form; tone rules stated across morpheme boundaries. Dialect described: the jàà speech of Canton Yaouré Nord (Bouaflé).
new_statements.identity_note: Gadou 1992 describes the jàà variety of Canton Yaouré Nord (Bouaflé sub-prefecture); Lautenschlager 1992 (not opened) describes the Zégata variety. Both fall under yaou1238 (Glottolog lists no dialect glottocodes). Older names: Kanga-bonou, Yauré, Kwendré 'dialect'. Gadou pp. 13-15 traces the classification history (Tauxier, Westermann & Bryan, Prost, Welmers).

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the existing Gadou 1992 statement (four level tonemes, silent on stress). Note the four levels are labelled very high/high/mid/low here vs Gadou's haut/mi-haut/mi-bas/bas. The open copy at the SIL URL is the English edition 'Alphabets of Africa' (same 1993 UNESCO/SIL volume, 319 pp., image-only scan, scanned at 150 dpi); sil.org direct download could not be reached by automated download, the the Internet Archive 2022-06-06 capture was used.
new_statements.rule_in_words: One-page phoneme/grapheme chart with a four-level tone system (very high, high, mid unmarked, low) marked on the word; no mention of stress, accent or prominence anywhere on the page.
new_statements.identity_note: Hartell 1993 gives no dialect; its data were 'verified by Frank Lautenschlager, SIL Côte d'Ivoire', whose own sketch is of the Zégata parler. Gadou 1992 (the existing statement) describes the jàà parler of Canton Yaouré Sud, Bouaflé. Both are yaou1238.
